screens.title: Java Fundamentals: Variables, Data Types, and Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn the essential building blocks of any Java program: variables, the primitive data types that describe what those variables can hold, and the operators that let your code compute and make decisions. We begin with the key idea that Java is statically typed — every variable has a declared type that guides how the compiler and runtime handle values. You will see concrete examples of integer and floating-point types, the single 16-bit character type, and booleans for logic. We'll also work through both implicit conversions that are safe and explicit casts that may lose data, showing common mistakes like truncation and overflow. Finally, you'll practice arithmetic, assignment, increment/decrement, relational, and logical operators and learn how precedence and associativity determine evaluation order. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose appropriate primitive types, declare and initialize variables and constants, reason about casting, and predict the result of compound expressions. Consider how these fundamentals prevent bugs and make later object-oriented code more robust.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide your practice. First, you will identify and choose Java's primitive data types for different storage needs. That means knowing when to use byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean and understanding their memory and numeric characteristics. Second, you will declare and initialize variables correctly, including class-level and local variables, and you will use the final keyword to create constants where values must not change. Third, you will perform implicit and explicit type conversions, recognizing when widening happens safely and when narrowing requires an explicit cast that can truncate or overflow. Lastly on this page, you'll begin to use arithmetic and assignment operators in expressions and understand integer division behavior. Each objective pairs a specific skill with why it matters: using the right type avoids bugs, correct scope prevents access errors, safe casting prevents data loss, and operator awareness prevents surprising results. These are practical skills you will apply in the hands-on calculator activity later.

screens.title: Static typing and variables
screens.narratorSegment: Java being statically typed means every variable is declared with a specific type before you use it. That declaration acts like a contract: the compiler knows the kind of data you intend to store and can check for type errors early. In practice, this reduces runtime surprises and enforces clearer code. A variable itself is simply a named container in memory with an associated type. For example, declaring int age = 30 tells the compiler to allocate a 32-bit integer container named age and initialize it to 30. Scope matters: a variable declared inside a method is local to that method and disappears when the method finishes, while a variable declared at the class level is available to the whole object instance. Constants use the final keyword; once final double PI = 3.14159 is set, attempts to change PI will cause a compile error. A common misconception is to think static typing prevents all type-related bugs — it prevents many but not logical mistakes like overflow or unintended truncation. Practice declaring variables with clear names and types, and always consider scope and lifetime: will you need the value across methods, or only within a single procedure? Reflect: how does making types explicit help you reason about code correctness?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Static typing assigns types to variables at compile time, enabling early error detection and clearer contracts for data storage.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Static typing
What is a variable?
A named memory location with a declared type. The type determines what values the variable can hold and how the compiler treats operations on it.
Examples of declarations
int age = 30;
double price = 19.99;
char grade = 'A';
boolean isActive = true;
final double PI = 3.14159; // constant
Key Takeaway

Declare types early to catch mismatches and document intent; use final for immutable values.

Common mistake

Assuming a local variable is accessible outside its method. Scope is limited to where you declare it.

Scope and examples
Local variables live inside methods; instance variables live on the object. Use final for constants and uppercase naming for clarity.
Scenario

You store a user's age in an int when you only need whole years. If you need precise measurements, choose a floating-point type.

Why it matters

Choosing clear types and scopes reduces bugs and improves maintainability when your codebase grows and objects interact.

screens.title: Primitive data types — overview and categories
screens.narratorSegment: Java's primitive types are the language's smallest, non-object values. They are grouped into integers (byte, short, int, long), floating-point numbers (float, double), a single character type (char), and boolean for true/false logic. Each type has a fixed size and range; for example, int is a 32-bit signed integer commonly used for whole numbers, while long is 64-bit and used when int might overflow. For decimals, double is the default 64-bit option and is preferred when precision matters; float is 32-bit and requires an F suffix for literals. Char holds a single 16-bit Unicode character written in single quotes. Boolean holds true or false and underpins conditional expressions. A practical example: use int for counting items, double for currency calculations requiring decimals (with care), and char for single-character flags. A common misconception is that floats and doubles behave like exact decimals — they are binary floating-point and can introduce precision quirks. Always pick a type whose range and precision match your needs and remember literal suffix rules like 10000000000L for long and 3.14f for float. What decision will you make for counters versus precise measurements?

keyIdea.title: Primitive categories
keyIdea.text: Select a primitive by matching required range and precision: integers for counts, floats/doubles for decimals, char for single characters, boolean for logic.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Primitive Types
Integer types
byte (8-bit), short (16-bit), int (32-bit), long (64-bit). Use int for most counters; use long for very large values and append L to literals.
Example

int count = 150; long population = 8000000000L;

Pitfall

Choosing too small a type can overflow; casting a large value into byte can flip sign.

Floating-point, char, boolean
float (32-bit, suffix F), double (64-bit, default), char (16-bit Unicode), boolean (true/false). Prefer double for most decimal math.
Example

double price = 19.99; float temp = 98.6f; char letter = 'A'; boolean isActive = true;

Why it matters

Selecting float when you need double precision can introduce rounding errors; char supports Unicode characters for text handling.

screens.title: Integer types in detail
screens.narratorSegment: Integer types differ by size and range. byte is an 8-bit signed integer with range -128 to 127 and can help reduce memory in large arrays. short is 16-bit for slightly larger ranges. int is the default 32-bit signed integer and is the most commonly used for counts and indices. long is 64-bit for very large integer values; when you write a literal that should be long, append L, for example one hundred billion written as 100000000000L. The practical consequence is that using the wrong type either wastes memory or enables overflow errors. A common mistake is to omit the L for a literal that's too large for int; the compiler then treats it as an int literal and raises an error or truncation issue. Another pitfall is relying on byte or short for arithmetic: Java promotes operands to int in many arithmetic expressions, so results may be int even if operands were smaller. For example, adding two bytes may yield an int result requiring a cast to store back into a byte. The takeaway: use int unless you have a specific reason, and use L for long literals to clearly communicate intent.

keyIdea.title: Integer guidance
keyIdea.text: Prefer int for general use, use long with L for large values, and be cautious with arithmetic promotions on smaller types.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Integer Types
Sizes & Common uses
  • byte: 8-bit, -128 to 127 — memory efficient for large arrays
  • short: 16-bit — legacy or special formats
  • int: 32-bit — default for counters and indices
  • long: 64-bit — use when int might overflow; suffix with L
Example

long population = 8000000000L; // L is required for large literals

Promotion and casting
Arithmetic on small integer types is promoted to int. Assigning back to smaller types requires explicit casts and may overflow.
byte a = 100;
byte b = 30;
int sum = a + b; // promoted to int
byte small = (byte) (a + b); // explicit cast may overflow
Common mistake

Expecting arithmetic on bytes to remain byte. Java promotes to int, which can surprise beginners.

screens.title: Floating-point types, char and boolean
screens.narratorSegment: Floating-point types represent numbers with fractional parts. In Java, float is 32-bit single precision and requires an F suffix for literals such as 3.14f. Double is 64-bit double precision and is the default for decimal literals like 3.14. Double generally offers greater precision and is preferred for most calculations; float is used when memory is constrained or when interfacing with APIs that require it. Important: floating-point arithmetic uses binary fractions, so not all decimal values are exact; that leads to small precision errors and explains why equality checks on floats or doubles can be unreliable. For characters, char is a 16-bit Unicode unit and is written in single quotes, for example 'A' or '@'. Use char for single characters, not strings. Boolean holds true or false values and is the basis for conditional expressions and logical operations. A common trap is comparing floating-point values with ==; instead compare with an acceptable epsilon or design logic that avoids exact equality checks. Choosing the right floating-point type and being mindful of precision keeps numeric logic correct. Floating-point types, char and boolean means prefer double for numeric precision, add f for float literals, use epsilon comparisons for equality, char for single unicode characters, boolean for true/false.. In practical terms, precision, literal suffixes, unicode characters, and logical values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Floating & Logical
float vs double
double is the default and more precise. float requires an F suffix and is lower precision.
double x = 10.0;
float y = 3.14f;
// Prefer double for most calculations
Precision note

Floating-point values are approximate. Avoid direct equality checks; use a small epsilon for comparisons when needed.

char and boolean
char holds a single Unicode character; boolean holds true or false for conditions and control flow.
Examples

char letter = 'Z'; boolean isActive = false;

Why it matters

Use the correct primitive to avoid implicit promotions or logical errors in conditionals and text handling.

screens.title: Declaring variables, initialization and scope
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through code that shows declarations, initialization, scope, and final constants. The key idea: where you declare a variable controls who can use it and for how long. In the example code you will see local variables created inside main that are only available during execution of main. You will also see an instance variable declared at the class level which represents state on the object. The final keyword creates a compile-time constant that cannot be reassigned. A common trap is expecting a local variable to persist beyond its method or to be accessible across instances; that confuses lifetime and ownership. Read the code and notice the explicit initializations, the final constant named with uppercase, and the difference in visibility between instance and local variables. Practice: try converting a local variable to an instance field and see how code that used to access it fails to compile until you update references. This exercise builds a foundation for writing safe methods and predictable object behavior. Declaring variables, initialization and scope means declare variables with clear scope and use final for immutable values; local variables live only within their method.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Declaration pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare variables with clear scope and use final for immutable values; local variables live only within their method.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Declarations & Scope
Starter code
public class SimpleExample {
    // instance variable
    int instanceCount = 0;

    public void doWork() {
        // local variable, only inside this method
        int localValue = 5;
        System.out.println(localValue);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final double PI = 3.14159; // constant
        double radius = 2.0;
        double area = PI * radius * radius;
        System.out.println("Area: " + area);
    }
}
Explanation
  • instanceCount: accessible to methods of the object instance.
  • localValue: exists only during method execution.
  • PI: final constant; cannot be reassigned.
Key Takeaway

Choose scope deliberately: instance fields for state, locals for temporary values, final to protect constants.

screens.title: Type casting: implicit (widening) conversions
screens.narratorSegment: Implicit casting, or widening conversion, happens automatically when you assign a value from a smaller type to a larger type where no data will be lost. For example, assigning an int to a long or an int to a double is safe because the target can represent all values of the source type. The compiler performs these conversions without explicit syntax: int myInt = 100; long myLong = myInt; double myDouble = myInt; These are common when combining integer and floating-point code or when storing a result in a variable with a larger range. The benefit is simpler code and fewer explicit casts, but be mindful that implicit widening doesn't change the value semantics — it only changes storage. A misconception is thinking implicit casting rounds or alters precision; it simply represents the same numeric value in a type with a larger range or precision. Use widening to avoid repetitive casts, but when you need to reduce storage or convert to a type with smaller range, you must use explicit casting and accept the risk of data loss. Type casting: implicit (widening) conversions means implicit widening safely converts smaller types into larger types without losing information, for example int to long or int to double.. In practical terms, safe automatic conversions between compatible types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Widening cast

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Implicit Casting
Definition & examples
int i = 100;
long l = i;        // implicit: int to long
double d = i;      // implicit: int to double
When to use

When the target type can represent all source values and you want simpler, safer assignments.

Misconception

Implicit widening does not change the numerical value logically. It does not round floating values or magically add precision — it only changes the representation to a type with a larger range.

Scenario

When combining int counters with double calculations, rely on implicit widening to get the correct numeric domain without verbose casts.

screens.title: Type casting: explicit (narrowing) conversions and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Explicit casting is required when converting a larger type to a smaller type because the conversion can lose information. You write a cast using parentheses with the target type, for example int small = (int) bigDouble; A concrete example: double bigDouble = 9.78; int smallInt = (int) bigDouble; smallInt will be 9 because casting truncates the decimal part; it does not round. Another example is casting an int to byte: byte b = (byte) 130; This overflows the byte range and results in a negative value due to wrap-around; b will become -126. These behaviors cause bugs if you expect automatic rounding or safe narrowing. Always ask: can the target type represent every possible source value? If not, you must handle potential data loss explicitly, perhaps by checking ranges before casting or by using a larger target type. A common misconception is that a cast will 'round' the value; instead it truncates or wraps depending on range. The safe practice is to avoid unnecessary narrowing casts, and when required, validate values before casting. Type casting: explicit (narrowing) conversions and pitfalls means explicit casts can truncate or overflow. validate ranges and prefer larger types when accuracy matters.. In practical terms, manual casts, truncation, overflow, and the common mistakes to avoid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Examples & effects

byte b = (byte) 130; // overflow: b == -126 (wrap-around)

Expecting rounding on cast; instead the fractional part is truncated and large values wrap when outside the target range.

screens.title: Arithmetic operators and integer division
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic operators perform basic numeric computations. Addition, subtraction, and multiplication behave as expected across integers and floating-point types. Division, however, has an important distinction: when both operands are integers, division performs integer division and truncates the fractional part. For example, 10 / 3 yields 3, not 3.333. To get a floating-point result, ensure at least one operand is a float or double, for example 10.0 / 3 or (double)10 / 3. Modulo returns the remainder of integer division: 10 % 3 equals 1. Floating-point operands also support modulo-like remainder operations but with decimal behavior. A common error is assuming division automatically produces the most precise result; the operand types determine the operation. Use explicit casts or floating literals when you need fractional results. This understanding is crucial in algorithms where rounding errors or truncation change program logic, such as index calculations, averages, or scaling factors. Ask yourself: which operand types will your expression use, and will integer division silently truncate values you need? Integer vs floating division
Examples:
int a = 10, b = 3;
System.out.println(a / b);   // prints 3 (integer division)

screens.title: Assignment, compound assignment, and increment/decrement
screens.narratorSegment: Assignment operators set or update variable values. The simple assignment uses equals, while compound assignments combine operation and assignment, for example count += 2 is shorthand for count = count + 2. They can be clearer and slightly more concise. Increment and decrement operators increase or decrease a value by one. The prefix form changes the value before it is used in an expression, while the postfix form returns the original value and then changes it. For instance, int i = 5; int j = i++; j gets 5 and i becomes 6; but if you use int k = ++i; then i becomes 7 and k gets 7. This distinction matters when these operators appear inside larger expressions, and misunderstanding it can cause off-by-one bugs. Use compound assignments for concise updates and be careful with ++ and -- when used in expressions. A safe practice is to keep increments as standalone statements unless you deliberately need their value inside an expression. Predictability improves when statements are simple and side effects are minimized. Compound assignments

Prefix vs Postfix

screens.title: Relational and logical operators, safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Relational operators compare values and return boolean results: equal, not equal, greater than, and so on. Use them to build conditions in if statements and loops. Logical operators combine boolean expressions: && for logical AND, || for logical OR, and! for NOT. Java's && and || are short-circuiting: for &&, if the first operand is false the second is not evaluated; for ||, if the first operand is true the second is skipped. Short-circuiting can improve performance and prevent errors such as NullPointerExceptions when the second operand relies on non-null objects. Safety notes: never use == to compare String content since == checks reference equality, not content. For floating-point numbers avoid exact equality; instead compare the absolute difference against a small epsilon. A typical mistake is writing complex combined conditions without parentheses and misreading the order of evaluation. Use parentheses to document intent and protect against precedence misunderstandings. The practical outcome is more reliable conditional logic and fewer annoying edge-case bugs. Operators & examples

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn the essential building blocks of any Java program: variables, the primitive data types that describe what those variables can hold, and the operators that let your code compute and make decisions. We begin with the key idea that Java is statically typed — every variable has a declared type that guides how the compiler and runtime handle values. You will see concrete examples of integer and floating-point types, the single 16-bit character type, and booleans for logic. We'll also work through both implicit conversions that are safe and explicit casts that may lose data, showing common mistakes like truncation and overflow. Finally, you'll practice arithmetic, assignment, increment/decrement, relational, and logical operators and learn how precedence and associativity determine evaluation order. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose appropriate primitive types, declare and initialize variables and constants, reason about casting, and predict the result of compound expressions. Consider how these fundamentals prevent bugs and make later object-oriented code more robust.

These learning objectives guide your practice. First, you will identify and choose Java's primitive data types for different storage needs. That means knowing when to use byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean and understanding their memory and numeric characteristics. Second, you will declare and initialize variables correctly, including class-level and local variables, and you will use the final keyword to create constants where values must not change. Third, you will perform implicit and explicit type conversions, recognizing when widening happens safely and when narrowing requires an explicit cast that can truncate or overflow. Lastly on this page, you'll begin to use arithmetic and assignment operators in expressions and understand integer division behavior. Each objective pairs a specific skill with why it matters: using the right type avoids bugs, correct scope prevents access errors, safe casting prevents data loss, and operator awareness prevents surprising results. These are practical skills you will apply in the hands-on calculator activity later.

This second objectives slide emphasizes applied skills you'll practice. First, you'll choose the right integer or floating-point type based on range and precision requirements and learn the syntax for long and float literals that distinguishes them at compile time. Second, you'll practice declaring constants with final and naming them clearly so values that shouldn't change are protected. Third, you'll master pre- and post-increment behavior so you can predict expression results when ++ or -- appears inside larger statements. Finally, you'll combine operators and parentheses to reason about precedence and associativity, and use parentheses to make intent explicit. Each of these applied objectives is included because small mistakes in literal suffixes, constants, or increment placement can cause subtle bugs. You will see short hands-on examples that mirror the SimpleCalculator activity later, ensuring you can both read and write expressions that behave as expected.

Java being statically typed means every variable is declared with a specific type before you use it. That declaration acts like a contract: the compiler knows the kind of data you intend to store and can check for type errors early. In practice, this reduces runtime surprises and enforces clearer code. A variable itself is simply a named container in memory with an associated type. For example, declaring int age = 30 tells the compiler to allocate a 32-bit integer container named age and initialize it to 30. Scope matters: a variable declared inside a method is local to that method and disappears when the method finishes, while a variable declared at the class level is available to the whole object instance. Constants use the final keyword; once final double PI = 3.14159 is set, attempts to change PI will cause a compile error. A common misconception is to think static typing prevents all type-related bugs — it prevents many but not logical mistakes like overflow or unintended truncation. Practice declaring variables with clear names and types, and always consider scope and lifetime: will you need the value across methods, or only within a single procedure? Reflect: how does making types explicit help you reason about code correctness?

Java's primitive types are the language's smallest, non-object values. They are grouped into integers (byte, short, int, long), floating-point numbers (float, double), a single character type (char), and boolean for true/false logic. Each type has a fixed size and range; for example, int is a 32-bit signed integer commonly used for whole numbers, while long is 64-bit and used when int might overflow. For decimals, double is the default 64-bit option and is preferred when precision matters; float is 32-bit and requires an F suffix for literals. Char holds a single 16-bit Unicode character written in single quotes. Boolean holds true or false and underpins conditional expressions. A practical example: use int for counting items, double for currency calculations requiring decimals (with care), and char for single-character flags. A common misconception is that floats and doubles behave like exact decimals — they are binary floating-point and can introduce precision quirks. Always pick a type whose range and precision match your needs and remember literal suffix rules like 10000000000L for long and 3.14f for float. What decision will you make for counters versus precise measurements?

Integer types differ by size and range. byte is an 8-bit signed integer with range -128 to 127 and can help reduce memory in large arrays. short is 16-bit for slightly larger ranges. int is the default 32-bit signed integer and is the most commonly used for counts and indices. long is 64-bit for very large integer values; when you write a literal that should be long, append L, for example one hundred billion written as 100000000000L. The practical consequence is that using the wrong type either wastes memory or enables overflow errors. A common mistake is to omit the L for a literal that's too large for int; the compiler then treats it as an int literal and raises an error or truncation issue. Another pitfall is relying on byte or short for arithmetic: Java promotes operands to int in many arithmetic expressions, so results may be int even if operands were smaller. For example, adding two bytes may yield an int result requiring a cast to store back into a byte. The takeaway: use int unless you have a specific reason, and use L for long literals to clearly communicate intent.

Floating-point types represent numbers with fractional parts. In Java, float is 32-bit single precision and requires an F suffix for literals such as 3.14f. Double is 64-bit double precision and is the default for decimal literals like 3.14. Double generally offers greater precision and is preferred for most calculations; float is used when memory is constrained or when interfacing with APIs that require it. Important: floating-point arithmetic uses binary fractions, so not all decimal values are exact; that leads to small precision errors and explains why equality checks on floats or doubles can be unreliable. For characters, char is a 16-bit Unicode unit and is written in single quotes, for example 'A' or '@'. Use char for single characters, not strings. Boolean holds true or false values and is the basis for conditional expressions and logical operations. A common trap is comparing floating-point values with ==; instead compare with an acceptable epsilon or design logic that avoids exact equality checks. Choosing the right floating-point type and being mindful of precision keeps numeric logic correct. Floating-point types, char and boolean means prefer double for numeric precision, add f for float literals, use epsilon comparisons for equality, char for single unicode characters, boolean for true/false.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Relational operators compare values and return boolean results: equal, not equal, greater than, and so on. Use them to build conditions in if statements and loops. Logical operators combine boolean expressions: && for logical AND, || for logical OR, and! for NOT. Java's && and || are short-circuiting: for &&, if the first operand is false the second is not evaluated; for ||, if the first operand is true the second is skipped. Short-circuiting can improve performance and prevent errors such as NullPointerExceptions when the second operand relies on non-null objects. Safety notes: never use == to compare String content since == checks reference equality, not content. For floating-point numbers avoid exact equality; instead compare the absolute difference against a small epsilon. A typical mistake is writing complex combined conditions without parentheses and misreading the order of evaluation. These are the three central concepts to retain. First, primitive data types define the size and representation of values in Java; choose types by range and precision. Second, variables are typed named containers with scope that controls lifetime; use final for constants you never want to change. Third, casting and operators determine how values are converted and combined; implicit widening is safe, explicit narrowing can truncate or overflow, and operator types and precedence determine expression results. Keep these concepts in mind when you write code: choose appropriate types, declare variables with clear scope, validate casts explicitly, and avoid assumptions about division or equality. A good habit is to add parentheses to clarify intent and to test expressions with example values so you can predict behavior.
